### Can the planner be a different model?

Yes. The planner field writes [agent] planner_model: another magpie model, one of Reasonix's own, or off.

### I changed it and Reasonix didn't notice. Why?

Reasonix reads global settings at startup. Start a new Studio or CLI process; a model set for a project or session also overrides the global one.

### Will my own providers and keys change?

No. magpie adds and removes only the provider named magpie and MAGPIE_REASONIX_API_KEY, and stops with an error on a same-named entry it didn't make.

More agents on the same models: [jcode on any model](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/jcode), [Crush on any model](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/crush), [Models in OpenCode](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/opencode-models) and [AtomCode on any model](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/atomcode). Something fails? See [Fixing common errors](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/troubleshooting), or ask on [Discord](https://discord.gg/vGSnD3ZKQF).

---

Source: https://usemagpie.ai/docs/atomcode

# AtomCode on any model

AtomCode is a Rust terminal coding agent on AtomGit (atomgit.com/atomgit_atomcode/atomcode). Its models live in `config.toml`: a `[models."…"]` table names a `[provider_accounts.…]` table, the shape AtomCode's own CodingPlan sign-in writes since 5.0.7. magpie writes the same shape, a magpie account and one table per model, so AtomCode can use any model you have in magpie: DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, Qwen, GPT or a ChatGPT subscription.

## Set up AtomCode

1. **Open magpie's Agents page.** Find the AtomCode row. Its list has the models you set up in AtomCode yourself, and the ones via magpie.
2. **Pick a magpie model.** magpie writes the account and model tables and points `default_provider` and `default_model` at your pick; with both set, AtomCode goes by `default_model`.
3. **Restart atomcode.** AtomCode reads its settings at start-up, so reopen any running session.

```
magpie atomcode deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro
magpie atomcode effort high
```

## What magpie writes

AtomCode's folder is `ATOMCODE_HOME` (an absolute path), else `~/.atomcode`. An AtomCode in WSL uses Linux's `~/.atomcode`, with the gateway as the distro reaches it. magpie writes:

```
# ~/.atomcode/config.toml
default_provider = "magpie/deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro"
default_model = "magpie/deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro"

[provider_accounts."magpie"]
provider = "openai-compatible"
base_url = "http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1"
api_key = "…"

[models."magpie/deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro"]
account = "magpie"
model = "deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro"
context_window = …
max_tokens = …
supports_vision = false
reasoning_effort_levels = ["…"]
```

The account uses `openai-compatible`, AtomCode's documented preset for a custom endpoint, at magpie's gateway `/v1`, with a key magpie issues to AtomCode alone. A model table's key is `magpie/<provider>/<model>`, and its `model` goes to the gateway as written. Each carries the context window (AtomCode compacts as it nears it; 128000 when magpie doesn't know it), the output limit (never above the window), image support and the effort levels on offer. When magpie's models change, magpie rewrites its own tables; your own model tables and legacy `providers.*` entries are left alone.

Requests are Chat Completions with Bearer auth and a User-Agent of `atomcode/<version>`; the key is AtomCode's own, so magpie knows a request is AtomCode's even when the header is changed.

## Effort

Effort is the current model table's `reasoning_effort`, sent with every request to it and kept per model. magpie picks none for you, so the vendor's default stands until you do. Only the levels that model supports (some of low, medium, high, xhigh, max) are offered.

## When it takes effect

AtomCode reads its settings at start-up. While atomcode is running, magpie tells you to restart open atomcode sessions.

## Switching back

Switching back removes magpie's account and model tables and puts back the `default_provider` and `default_model` you had before, where AtomCode still has that model (otherwise they go). Picking one of your own AtomCode models in magpie also removes magpie's tables.

```
magpie atomcode default
```

## FAQ

### How do I use DeepSeek, GLM or a ChatGPT subscription in AtomCode?

On magpie's Agents page, pick a via-magpie model for AtomCode. magpie adds [provider_accounts."magpie"] and one [models."magpie/…"] table per model to ~/.atomcode/config.toml and points the defaults at your pick.

### What context window does AtomCode get?

magpie writes each model's context_window, or 128000 when it doesn't know it. AtomCode compacts as it nears the window.

### I changed it and AtomCode didn't notice. Why?

AtomCode reads its settings at start-up. Restart the open atomcode sessions.

### Do my own defaults come back when I switch back?

Yes. magpie stashes default_provider and default_model when it steps in and puts them back when it steps out, where AtomCode still has that model.

More agents on the same models: [Reasonix Studio on any model](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/reasonix), [jcode on any model](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/jcode), [Crush on any model](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/crush) and [Shelley on any model](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/shelley). Something fails? See [Fixing common errors](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/troubleshooting), or ask on [Discord](https://discord.gg/vGSnD3ZKQF).

---

Source: https://usemagpie.ai/docs/shelley

# Shelley on any model

Shelley (boldsoftware/shelley) is the coding agent for exe.dev, a web app that `shelley serve` runs. Its models live in its database, not in a file magpie can edit, so magpie tells it through the same API Shelley's own Models and Profiles pages use: a custom model at magpie's gateway, made the default. New Shelley conversations then run on any model you have in magpie: DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, Qwen, GPT or a ChatGPT subscription.

## Set up Shelley

1. **Start Shelley first.** magpie talks to a running Shelley. When it isn't running, magpie says so: start `shelley serve` and try again.
2. **Pick a model on magpie's Agents page.** Shelley's row lists the models Shelley can use itself and the ones via magpie. Pick one of the latter.
3. **Start a new conversation.** New conversations start on the default profile's model, the one you just picked.

```
shelley serve                              # Shelley must be running
magpie shelley deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro
```

## How magpie tells Shelley

Shelley opens a Unix socket for its CLI: `$SHELLEY_SOCKET`, else `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/shelley/shelley.sock` (`~/.config/shelley` by default, on a Mac too), or `shelley-2.sock` and on when a second server took the first. magpie tries them in the order Shelley's CLI does and calls `/api/custom-models` and `/api/profiles`:

```
POST /api/custom-models   (over ~/.config/shelley/shelley.sock)
{
  "display_name": "deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro (magpie)",
  "provider_type": "openai",
  "endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1",
  "api_key": "…",
  "model_name": "deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro",
  "reasoning_support": "yes",
  "image_support": "no",
  "max_tokens": …
}
```

Each model you pick in magpie is a custom model of type openai at the gateway's `/v1` (Shelley adds `/chat/completions`), with a key magpie issues to Shelley alone. Shelley usually learns reasoning and image support from models.dev by endpoint and name, which magpie's models aren't in, so magpie says what it knows. Then magpie sets the default profile's `model` to it; for a model that doesn't reason it clears `thinking_level`, which Shelley would refuse.

magpie keeps the ids of the models it made, so a model you made by hand at the gateway stays yours. When the gateway's address changes, magpie updates its models.

## Which conversations change

New conversations use the new model; an open one keeps its model until you pick another in its model menu. magpie says so after the switch.

## Switching back

Switching back puts the default profile's model and thinking level back to what they were (or to the server's default when that model can't be used any more), then deletes every custom model magpie made. You can also pick one of Shelley's own models in magpie. If Shelley was uninstalled, magpie notes it and takes its models out when Shelley runs again.

```
magpie shelley default
```

## FAQ

### How do I use DeepSeek, GLM or a ChatGPT subscription in Shelley?

Run shelley serve, then pick a via-magpie model for Shelley on magpie's Agents page. magpie adds an openai custom model at its gateway to Shelley and makes it the default profile's model.

### Why does magpie say Shelley isn't running?

Shelley's models are in its database, which magpie changes only through a running Shelley's socket. Start shelley serve and try again.

### Why is an open conversation still on the old model?

The default profile applies to new conversations. Change an open one in its own model menu.

### Will my own custom models be deleted?

No. magpie deletes only the model ids it made; one you made by hand, even at the gateway, stays yours.

More agents on the same models: [AtomCode on any model](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/atomcode), [Reasonix Studio on any model](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/reasonix), [jcode on any model](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/jcode) and [Cindy on any model](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/cindy). Something fails? See [Fixing common errors](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/troubleshooting), or ask on [Discord](https://discord.gg/vGSnD3ZKQF).

---

Source: https://usemagpie.ai/docs/cindy

# Cindy on any model

Cindy is a desktop app that runs Claude Code, Codex and Pi. It keeps its providers in its own database, their keys encrypted, and takes a new one only through its own import link, which you confirm in Cindy. So magpie writes nothing into Cindy: it gives Cindy an import link with magpie as one custom provider, an endpoint for each runtime. Claude Code, Codex and Pi in Cindy then run on any model in magpie: DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, Qwen, an OpenAI or Anthropic key, and the ChatGPT or Copilot subscription you signed in to.

## Add magpie to Cindy

1. **Open Cindy once.** Once Cindy has run, its data folder is there (`~/Library/Application Support/Cindy` on a Mac, `CindyGlobal` for its global build) and magpie's Agents page lists it.
2. **Add a provider in magpie.** Add an API key on the Providers page, or sign in to a subscription.
3. **Click Add magpie.** On Cindy's row, click Add magpie; magpie hands the import link to Cindy.
4. **Confirm it in Cindy.** Nothing is added until you do. Then pick a model from the Magpie provider for Claude Code, Codex or Pi in Cindy.

If nothing happens, nothing on this computer opens Cindy's links (`cindy://`), or the program that registered them was moved. magpie checks for that first and says why instead of doing nothing: open Cindy once or install it again, then click again.

## What the link holds

The link's `data` is base64url-encoded JSON. Decoded, it is:

```
cindy://provider/import?v=1&data=
{
  "kind": "custom", "name": "Magpie", "id": "magpie",
  "auth": {"method": "apiKey", "apiKey": "…"},
  "endpoints": [
    {"protocol": "anthropic-messages", "baseUrl": "http://127.0.0.1:3425",
     "targets": ["claude-code"], "modelsUrl": "http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1/models"},
    {"protocol": "openai-responses", "baseUrl": "http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1",
     "targets": ["codex"], "modelsUrl": "http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1/models"},
    {"protocol": "openai-chat", "baseUrl": "http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1",
     "targets": ["pi"], "modelsUrl": "http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1/models"}
  ]
}
```

Claude Code speaks Anthropic Messages at the gateway itself; Codex speaks OpenAI Responses and Pi OpenAI Chat, both at the gateway's `/v1`. Each endpoint lists its models from the gateway's `/v1/models`, so a provider you add to magpie later shows up when Cindy fetches models again.

## From the command line

```
magpie cindy add      # opens Cindy to add magpie; confirm it there
```

The command prints the link it opened. When nothing here can open it, it says why rather than reporting success.

## How magpie knows it was added

magpie reads Cindy's databases read-only: one per account (`cindy-<account>.db`) once you sign in, `cindy-local-v1.db` before. When any of them has a custom provider with the id or name magpie, or the gateway's address in its endpoints, the row says it's added. It can read them while Cindy runs, and never writes them. When a database can't be read, magpie says it doesn't know, not that it isn't added.

## Usage and keys

The key in the link is Cindy's own, so its requests are counted as Cindy's in magpie's usage, apart from other agents.

## FAQ

### Can Claude Code in Cindy use DeepSeek or GLM?

Yes. Once magpie is added to Cindy, Claude Code uses any model in magpie, DeepSeek and GLM included, through the Magpie provider's Anthropic endpoint.

### Does magpie change Cindy's settings?

No. Cindy takes a new provider only through its own import link, which you confirm in Cindy. magpie only reads Cindy's databases to show whether magpie was added.

### Add magpie does nothing. What now?

Nothing on this computer opens cindy:// links, or the program that registered them is gone. Open Cindy once or install it again, then click again; magpie says which it is.

### Cindy isn't on magpie's Agents page.

magpie lists Cindy once it has run on this computer and made its data folder. Open Cindy once, then look again.

More desktop apps on the same models: [AionUi on any model](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/aionui), [Every model in Cherry Studio, through magpie](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/cherry-studio) and [Shelley on any model](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/shelley). Something fails? See [Fixing common errors](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/troubleshooting), or ask on [Discord](https://discord.gg/vGSnD3ZKQF).

---

Source: https://usemagpie.ai/docs/cherry-studio

# Every model in Cherry Studio, through magpie

Cherry Studio is a desktop chat client that takes any OpenAI-compatible provider. magpie adds itself there as one provider, named magpie, so every model you have in magpie shows up in Cherry Studio: providers with an API key and the Claude, ChatGPT or Copilot subscriptions you signed in to.

magpie runs a gateway on your computer at `http://127.0.0.1:3425`. It speaks the OpenAI Chat Completions API and translates each request for the provider behind the model, Anthropic’s, Google’s or a subscription’s, with streaming, tool calls and reasoning. Cherry Studio sees one OpenAI-compatible provider at `http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1`.

Cherry Studio keeps its providers in its own database, and magpie never writes to it. It adds itself through Cherry Studio’s add-provider link instead, and you confirm it in Cherry Studio. This works in Cherry Studio 1.x and 2.x.

## Add magpie to Cherry Studio

1. **Add providers in magpie.** In the Providers tab, add an API key (DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen, OpenRouter…) or sign in to a subscription.
2. **Open the Agents tab.** magpie lists Cherry Studio once it has run on this computer, including a data folder you moved elsewhere.
3. **Click Add magpie.** On Cherry Studio’s row, press Add magpie. Cherry Studio opens its model provider settings with magpie filled in: name magpie, type OpenAI, the gateway’s address and a key.
4. **Confirm it in Cherry Studio.** Nothing is added until you do.

If nothing opens, no app on this computer handles Cherry Studio’s links yet: open Cherry Studio once, or install it again, then click Add magpie again.

## Pick the models

Cherry Studio lists a provider’s models from `/v1/models`, so the magpie provider offers every model magpie has, named `provider/model` (for example `deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro`). Add the ones you want to the magpie provider in Cherry Studio, and choose them in a chat like any other model.

A provider you add in magpie later shows up the next time Cherry Studio fetches the list; there is nothing to change in Cherry Studio. Several accounts behind one model, rest periods after a 429 and failover work as they do for every agent.

## From a terminal

```
magpie cherrystudio add      # opens Cherry Studio to add magpie, confirm it there
```

`cherry-studio` works as the name too.

## How magpie knows it was added

Once Cherry Studio has a provider at the gateway’s address, the row shows magpie instead of the button. magpie reads Cherry Studio 2.x’s database for this, read-only. Cherry Studio 1.x keeps providers where magpie doesn’t read them, so there the button stays.

## Usage and keys

On a gateway that isn’t shared, the key in the link is Cherry Studio’s own, so its requests are counted as Cherry Studio’s in magpie’s Usage, apart from your coding agents. When the gateway is shared on your network with gateway keys, the link carries a key that works there.

## FAQ

### Do I need an API key to use Claude or ChatGPT in Cherry Studio?

No. Sign in to a Claude, ChatGPT or Copilot subscription in magpie, and its models appear in the magpie provider in Cherry Studio.

### Does magpie change Cherry Studio’s settings?

No. magpie opens Cherry Studio’s own add-provider dialog, and you confirm it. It only reads Cherry Studio’s database to show whether magpie was added.

### What address and type does the magpie provider use?

Type OpenAI, at http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1, or the gateway address you set in magpie.

### Why don’t I see a new model in Cherry Studio?

Cherry Studio shows models you added to the provider. Fetch the magpie provider’s model list again and add the new one.

### Cherry Studio isn’t in magpie’s Agents tab.

magpie lists it once Cherry Studio has run on this computer. Open Cherry Studio once, then look again.

Another desktop app on the same models: [AionUi on any model](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/aionui). Using a coding agent too? See [Subscriptions in any agent](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/subscriptions) and [Get started](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/start). Something fails? See [Fixing common errors](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/troubleshooting), or ask on [Discord](https://discord.gg/vGSnD3ZKQF).

---

Source: https://usemagpie.ai/docs/troubleshooting

# Fixing common errors: 401, 429, 502, 504 and more

An error from magpie’s gateway says what went wrong in its own words. This page lists the common ones, what causes them, and the fix.

Every request is listed on magpie’s Routing page, with which provider and account it went to and how each try ended. Copy Report on a request copies what you need to ask for help.

## 401 and 403: a key or sign-in refused

**From the vendor.** The provider turned down the key or sign-in magpie sent. magpie sets that key or account aside and tries the next one, so you see the error only when none is left. A sign-in that has run out says so, for example “the ChatGPT sign-in has expired — sign in again”.

- **Fix:.** sign in again from ＋ Add provider (or `magpie accounts add <provider>`), or give the provider a new key.

**From magpie itself.** magpie answers 403 on its own in a few cases, before anything is sent:

| Error | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| model disabled | You turned the model off in magpie. | Turn it on again on its provider. |
| model not allowed for the gateway key | The gateway key is held to some models. | `magpie gateway-key models <id>` lists or changes them. |
| magpie doesn’t answer the web page … | A web page called the gateway from a browser. | List it in Settings › Network and sharing › Web pages, and send a gateway key. |

## 429 and rest periods

A 429 means the provider is out of quota, out of credit or rate limiting you. magpie rests the key or account that was refused and sends the request to the next account, the next member of a routing group, or the provider’s Fallback. The provider’s row shows Resting · {why} · back at {time}.

| Refused for | Rests |
| --- | --- |
| Quota, with a reset time | Until the reset |
| Rate limit, with Retry-After | Until then |
| Credit | 30 minutes, then 2 hours, 8 hours, a day, 3 days and a week if it is refused again |
| A ChatGPT account out of credits | Until the reset its refusal names, else until its full window renews, else 5 hours |
| Any other failure | A minute, doubling on repeats up to 10 minutes (30 for a rate limit) |

- **Ask it again now..** Try now ends the rest: the next request asks it again. Refused again, it rests again.
- **Cap the rest..** `magpie provider rest-cap <id> 4h` sets the longest rest for a provider; `off` stops it resting for failures that say nothing of why.
- **A relay whose limits pass in a moment..** Untick Set it aside when out of quota or rate limited in the provider editor’s Advanced: a 429 then rests nothing, and the next request goes to it as usual.
- **Never all at once..** Add a second account or a fallback model, so a spent one never stops the agent. `magpie accounts` shows how much of each account’s allowance is used.

Rests are kept across restarts, so quitting magpie doesn’t bring a resting account back early.

## 502: the provider didn’t answer

A 502 means magpie couldn’t get an API reply from the provider. What follows the provider’s name says which case it is:

- **“didn’t answer: …”.** The connection failed: a name that doesn’t resolve, a refused connection, a proxy that is down. When this computer has no network at all, magpie notices and rests nobody.
- **“… not an API reply”.** The provider answered, but with a web page (a sign-in page, a Cloudflare challenge), nothing at all, or something that isn’t JSON. The base URL usually points at a web site instead of the API: check it against the vendor’s docs, and whether it should end in `/v1`.
- **OpenCode: “… which is no error, not an API reply”..** OpenCode’s gateway sometimes answers a 400 holding only the model’s name. The same request is answered some seconds later, so magpie reads it as a 502, asks again within the request’s patience or tries a group’s next member, and rests nobody. It is tied to requests carrying very large tool lists.

A 502, 503, 504, 529 or Cloudflare’s 520 to 524 counts as busy: magpie asks again or moves to a routing group’s next member before the agent sees it.

## 504: no answer in time

- **“<provider>: no first token in Ns”..** A routing group gives each member a time to start answering (First token). The member was slower, so the next was asked. Raise it on the group for a slow model.
- **“no member of the group answered within its Ns budget”..** Every member of the group was tried within the group’s time and none answered.
- **“magpie held this request for … without routing it to any provider”..** The request waited inside magpie and was stopped rather than left waiting. Send it again; if it comes back, Copy Report on that request on the Routing page and share it.

## Model not found (404)

The error reads *magpie knows no model “…”*, often with *did you mean …?* and the list of your provider ids.

- **Name it as magpie does..** Use `provider/model`, as `magpie models` lists it, a routing group’s id or name, or a bare model id.
- **“… is switched off in Magpie, so … is not served”..** The provider or routing group is off. Switch it on again on the Providers or Routing page.
- **No providers yet..** The error says “add a provider in magpie first”.

## The agent doesn’t show the model

- **Restart the agent..** Most agents read their config only when they start. magpie says so on the agent’s row after a change, for example “Codex builds its model list at start-up”. Codex’s app also keeps an app-server running; restart it as the notice says.
- **Check magpie serves it..** `magpie models` lists every model you can pick. A model you turned off, or one whose provider is switched off, isn’t listed.
- **Claude Code..** `/model` lists magpie’s models marked “via magpie”. If `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK` or `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX` is set in your shell, Claude Code goes to that cloud instead of magpie; remove it from your shell profile.

## Port 3425 is in use

The gateway listens on `127.0.0.1:3425`. To move it, open Settings › Network and sharing › Gateway address. Only the port is set there, 1024 to 65535, and the agents magpie connected move with it.

| magpie says | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Port … is in use by another program: pick another one | Pick a free port. |
| Another magpie serves the gateway at …: set its port there, or quit it first | Two copies of magpie are running. Quit one. |
| Port … is taken by another program, magpie web perhaps: magpie tries again every few seconds | Find what holds the port, or move the gateway to another. |
| MAGPIE_ADDR=… sets the gateway’s whole address, host:port: unset it to set the port here | Unset `MAGPIE_ADDR`, or change it. |

## Agents in WSL

On Windows, magpie looks in running WSL distros for agents such as Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Kimi Code and Qwen Code. Each one it finds gets a row of its own on the Agents page, and magpie sets it up as it does on Windows. It never starts a stopped distro.

- **The agent isn’t listed..** Start the distro, and check Settings › General › Detect agents in WSL is on.
- **It can’t reach magpie..** Under WSL’s default NAT networking, magpie also serves the gateway at Windows’ address on the WSL network, with a key of its own, and writes that address into the agent’s config. With mirrored networking the agent uses `127.0.0.1` as on Windows. Windows’ firewall still decides: WSL’s network counts as Public, so allow magpie there if the connection is blocked.
- **A change doesn’t show..** An agent in WSL reads its config at start-up: restart it there.

## From another computer on the network

By default the gateway answers only this computer. To use it from another: Settings › Network and sharing › Share on local network. The other computer sends a gateway key from the Gateway page’s Gateway keys.

- **“magpie isn’t shared on the local network”..** Turn sharing on, on the computer that runs magpie.
- **401..** The key is missing, off or expired. Send an enabled gateway key as `Authorization: Bearer <key>` or `x-api-key`.
- **403 for a model..** The key is held to some models: `magpie gateway-key models <id>`.

Don’t open the port to the internet; use a VPN between your computers. The full setup, another magpie included, is in [Remote magpie](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/remote).

## A subscription moved to a plugin isn’t served

Command Code, Cursor, Devin, Factory, Grok, Kiro, Xiaomi MiMo, Qoder, WorkBuddy, ZCode and Zed are no longer built into magpie. Each is served by a community plugin that does the same job. Accounts added before still need to move to the plugin, and nothing serves them until they do.

- **Fix:.** a line over the Providers list says “… built-in subscription is retired, and its accounts haven’t moved to its plugin yet”. Press Move to the plugin: magpie installs the plugin and checks each account. Moving keeps your accounts, models and agents as they are. magpie also moves them by itself, and installing the plugin from the Plugins page does too.

An error after the move comes from the plugin, which does the sign-in, models and requests.

## FAQ

### Why does magpie answer 502 when the provider is up?

The provider answered with something that isn’t an API reply, such as a web page or an empty body. The base URL usually points at the vendor’s web site instead of its API.

### Why does an account stay unused after a 429?

magpie rests it until the reset the vendor named, or for a while if none was named. The provider’s row says when it is back, and Try now ends the rest.

### What does “magpie knows no model” mean?

No provider serves a model by that name. Name it as provider/model, as magpie models lists it, or switch its provider on again.

### How do I change magpie’s port?

Settings › Network and sharing › Gateway address. The agents magpie connected move with it.

### Can an agent in WSL use magpie on Windows?

Yes. magpie finds agents in running WSL distros and sets each up with an address it can reach. Under NAT networking, Windows’ firewall must let WSL’s connection through.

### Can I use magpie from another computer?

Yes. Turn on Settings › Network and sharing › Share on local network, and send a gateway key from the other computer. Don’t open the port to the internet.

Still stuck? Copy the request’s report from the Routing page and ask on [Discord](https://discord.gg/vGSnD3ZKQF).

---

Source: https://usemagpie.ai/docs/library

# Library

magpie’s Library keeps instructions, MCP servers, skills, hooks and subagents in one place, and writes each of them into every agent you tick for it, in that agent’s own files and format. The agents read those files as they always do. magpie adds no layer between an agent and what it is given: the agent itself decides when to use a skill, an MCP tool or a subagent.

The page has seven tabs: Instructions, MCP servers, Skills, Hooks, Subagents, RTK and billion-context. Each item has a row of agents; tick an agent to give it the item, untick it to take it away. An agent reads the change when it starts again.

## Where it is kept

- **The library.** is `library.json` in magpie’s config folder (`~/.config/magpie`, or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/magpie` when that is set). Instruction texts and skill folders are in `library/` next to it.
- **Every change.** saves the library and writes it into every agent at once. magpie records what it wrote, so it only ever takes away its own entries and leaves yours alone.
- **Backups..** Before a change, the files it replaces are copied to `backups/` in the same folder. The last 30 are kept. The Backups button at the top of each tab opens them.
- **Write it again..** After you install an agent, or edit its files by hand, `magpie library sync` writes the library into every agent again.

```
magpie library          # what the library gives each agent
magpie library sync     # write it into the agents again
```

## Instructions

Instructions are text every session of an agent starts with, such as house rules or a coding style. magpie writes its part between two marker lines in the agent’s instructions file:

```
<!-- magpie:begin · written by magpie from its Library -->
…the Library's instructions…
<!-- magpie:end -->
```

Everything outside the markers is yours and is never changed. You can keep several named sets and give each set to different agents, and a set can live in a file of your own.

| Agent | File |
| --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` |
| Codex | `~/.codex/AGENTS.md` (or `AGENTS.override.md` when you use one) |
| Gemini CLI | `~/.gemini/GEMINI.md` |
| Antigravity | `~/.gemini/config/GEMINI.md` |
| OpenCode | `AGENTS.md` in its config folder |
| Copilot CLI | `~/.copilot/copilot-instructions.md` |
| Goose, Crush, Qwen Code, CodeBuddy | `.goosehints`, `CRUSH.md`, `QWEN.md`, `CODEBUDDY.md` |
| Droid, Grok, dsh, omp | `AGENTS.md` in the agent’s own folder |
| Pi, OmO | the first one there of `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` |

Folders follow the agent’s own setting: a custom `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` or `CODEX_HOME` is used in place of the default.

## MCP servers

An MCP server is either a command (a program the agent starts, such as `npx …`) or a URL (HTTP or SSE). magpie writes one entry per server into each ticked agent’s MCP config, in that agent’s format, and keeps any fields you added to the entry yourself.

| Agent | File |
| --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `~/.claude.json` |
| Codex | `~/.codex/config.toml` |
| Gemini CLI | `~/.gemini/settings.json` |
| Antigravity | `~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json` |
| OpenCode | `opencode.json` |
| Cursor | `~/.cursor/mcp.json` |
| Copilot CLI | `~/.copilot/mcp-config.json` |
| Zed | `context_servers` in its `settings.json` |

- **Variables..** `${NAME}` in a header or an env value is written in each agent’s own syntax. An agent that has no such syntax is not given that server, and the page says why.
- **SSE..** Codex, Goose, dsh, Grok, Command Code and Zed can’t use an SSE server. Claude Desktop takes no remote servers at all.
- **Single tools off..** You can turn off tools one by one for Codex, Gemini CLI, Crush, Hermes Agent, Claude Code and OpenCode, each in its own setting. Every other agent gets the whole server.
- **Sign-in..** A server that needs OAuth is signed in to once, in magpie. Agents then reach it through magpie’s gateway at `/mcp/<name>`.
- **This computer only..** Turn off Sync to your other computers for a server that should stay here (`magpie library mcp local <name> on`).

With the [MCP router](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/mcp-router) on, each agent gets one server named `magpie` in place of these entries, and magpie runs each command server once for all of them. It is off by default.

## Skills

A skill is a folder with a `SKILL.md` in it. The agent reads each skill’s name and description and loads the rest when a task needs it. Add one from GitHub, any git repository, a folder on this computer, or the market on the Skills tab.

| Agent | Folder |
| --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `~/.claude/skills` |
| Codex | `~/.codex/skills` |
| Gemini CLI | `~/.gemini/skills` |
| OpenCode | `skills` in its config folder |
| Cursor | `~/.cursor/skills` |
| Copilot CLI | `~/.copilot/skills` |
| Goose | `~/.agents/skills` |

### Links or copies

Give skills as sets how a skill reaches an agent, for every agent or, under By agent, for one:

- **Links.** (the default). The agent’s folder links to the library’s copy, so an update reaches every agent at once. On Windows without the right to make links, a junction is used.
- **Copies..** Each agent gets a folder of its own, for tools that don’t follow links. A copy is made again when the library’s skill changes. If the agent, or you, edit a copy, the next sync takes the newest edit into the library and gives it to the other agents. An edit that loses to a newer one is kept with the backups.

A skill folder of your own with the same name is never written over: the page asks whether to use the library’s or keep yours.

### Editing and updates

- **Edit.** opens a skill’s files on the page; Save (or ⌘S) writes them. The command line has no editor.
- **Updates..** When you open the Skills tab, skills from GitHub are checked for updates if 12 hours have passed since the last check (`magpie library skill update` checks now). A skill you changed is never replaced without asking.
- **Put skills in..** Skills go to each ticked agent’s own folder (the default), or also into `~/.agents/skills`, which Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Crush, Droid, Kimi Code and other tools read.
- **Off here..** A skill can be turned off on this computer only; a sync from another computer doesn’t turn it back on.

## Subagents

A subagent is a helper the main agent can hand a task to. It has a name, a description and a prompt. magpie writes it as a file in each ticked agent’s subagent folder. The main agent reads every subagent’s **description** and decides itself when to call one, so the description should say plainly what it is for and when to use it.

- **Name:.** 2 to 50 lowercase letters, digits and `-`. A few names are reserved, such as `default` and `main`.
- **Description:.** required, up to 1,000 characters.
- **Prompt:.** required. It becomes the subagent’s instructions.
- **Model:.** optional. See Subagent models.

| Agent | File | Skills, MCP servers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `~/.claude/agents/<name>.md` | the ones you pick |
| Codex | `~/.codex/agents/<name>.toml` | all the agent has |
| OpenCode | `agents/<name>.md` in its config folder | all the agent has |
| Gemini CLI | `~/.gemini/agents/<name>.md` | all the agent has |
| Qwen Code | `agents/<name>.md` in its folder | all the agent has |
| Droid | `~/.factory/droids/<name>.md` | MCP servers you pick; all skills |
| Grok | `agents/<name>.md` in its folder | all the agent has |
| Cursor | `~/.cursor/agents/<name>.md` | all the agent has |
| Copilot CLI | `~/.copilot/agents/<name>.agent.md` | all the agent has |

- Only Claude Code limits a subagent to the skills you pick, and only Claude Code and Droid to the MCP servers you pick. Elsewhere a subagent has everything its agent has.
- Cursor: only the Cursor app reads `~/.cursor/agents`. `cursor-agent` reads only a project’s `.cursor/agents`.
- Kimi Code, Goose, Crush, Qoder, CodeBuddy, iFlow and Kiro have no user-wide subagent folder, so they get none. Agents in WSL get none either.
- If you edit a file magpie wrote, it becomes yours and magpie stops changing it. A file of your own with the same name is never written over; the page shows a problem instead.

## Subagent models

A subagent’s Model field is written only for **Codex**. Every other agent runs its subagents on the model it picks itself, and the page says so. Left empty, the field reads Picked by the agent.

For Codex, the model goes into the subagent’s `.toml` file. Codex lays that file over the spawn, so requests carry that model and magpie’s gateway routes them like any other request. You can pick any model in Codex’s list, a magpie `provider/model`, or a routing group (`group/<id>`).

### Codex’s subagent model on the Agents page

Codex’s row on the Agents page has a subagent model of its own, for every subagent Codex starts:

- **Lead’s pick.** (the default). The main agent picks each subagent’s model, one of Codex’s own too. A subagent it names no model for runs on the main agent’s model. A resumed subagent stays on the model it started on.
- **Same as the lead..** Every subagent runs on the main agent’s model.
- **A model or a group..** Every subagent runs on it, even when the main agent names another.

> **The Agents page wins.** When that setting is anything but Lead’s pick, the gateway sends every Codex subagent request to it, over a Library subagent’s own model too. The Library editor then says so. Picking a model there also removes `default_subagent_model` from Codex’s config.

Codex’s own `[agents] default_subagent_model` in `config.toml` is a different thing: only the model a subagent starts on when the main agent names none. One exception to all of the above: a task the ChatGPT backend has sealed stays on the model it asked for, unless the setting is a ChatGPT account’s model.

Claude Code has its own order: the model the main agent names in its call, then the subagent file’s `model:`, then `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` (which Claude Code’s row on the Agents page can set), then the session’s model.

## Hooks

A hook is a command an agent runs at a point in its turn: a notification when it finishes, a formatter after it edits a file. Pick a portable event (turn end, after a tool, before a tool, on a prompt, at session start) and magpie writes it under each agent’s own name for that event. Only Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Grok Build and Grok App take hooks. A hook entry you change becomes yours.

## RTK

The RTK tab turns on [RTK](https://www.rtk-ai.app/) per agent: the agent’s shell commands run through RTK, which shortens their output to save tokens. magpie can install RTK for you; turning it off works with RTK gone.

## billion-context

The billion-context tab turns on [billion-context](https://github.com/ranxianglei/billion-context)’s plugin per agent: it folds older turns of a long session into summaries the model can open again, so the session stays inside the model’s window. It is offered for Pi, omp, OpenCode, Claude Code, Hermes, DeepSeek Harness and Zed, whose requests still go through magpie with it on. magpie can install it for you (`npm install -g billion-context --prefix=~/.local`) and runs its own installer and remover; turning it off puts back what the install changed in the agent’s settings. An agent turned on here can’t also run billion-context-pi or opencode-acp.

For Claude Code, billion-context’s install turns Claude Code’s own auto-compaction off. magpie turns it back on, so a session billion-context doesn’t fold, such as one in the Claude desktop app’s Code tab, compacts instead of stopping at “Prompt is too long”. A `DISABLE_AUTO_COMPACT` you set yourself is left as it is.

Zed has no billion-context plugin, and Hermes’ and DeepSeek Harness’ plugins only catch HTTPS traffic, which magpie’s local address isn’t. Turned on, magpie runs `bili start` and points the agent’s magpie provider at `http://127.0.0.1:8787/bili/` followed by magpie’s address, the route billion-context documents for any client; for Hermes and DeepSeek Harness, in every profile that has magpie’s provider. Pick one of magpie’s models for the agent on the Agents page first, and restart it after turning it on or off.

The card shows how many tokens billion-context saved, in its own count: the net savings its dashboard shows, after the rebuilds a fold causes and the summaries’ cost, with how many folds and sessions, over every session it ran on this computer. magpie asks a running billion-context for it (`/__bili/overview`); when none runs, the card shows the last count it read and when. It shows nothing until billion-context has run for an agent.

## What magpie touches

- Only what it wrote: the text between its markers, entries it recorded, files it marked as its own.
- Never a file, entry or skill of yours with the same name. The page shows the clash and lets you choose.
- Anything it replaces goes to the backups first.

Projects can get skills and MCP servers too, in the project’s own folders (such as `.claude/skills`, `.agents/skills`, `.mcp.json` or `.codex/config.toml`). From a terminal, `magpie library project add .` adds the folder you are in, `magpie library project skill add . pdf docx` gives it skills, `magpie library project skill rm . pdf` takes one away, and `magpie library project skills .` lists them.

---

Source: https://usemagpie.ai/docs/mcp-router

# MCP router

The MCP servers you add in magpie’s Library are normally written into each agent’s own config, one entry per server. With the **MCP router** on, each agent is given a single server named `magpie` instead, and magpie passes each call on to the Library server behind it. It is **off by default**.

- **Set up once..** A server written once in the Library reaches every agent and app through one entry.
- **Run once..** A command server (one started as a program, such as `npx …`) runs once in magpie, not once in each agent. A server with no calls for 10 minutes is stopped and starts again on the next call.
- **One address for other apps..** Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf or an app on another computer can connect to magpie and use every Library server.

Tools appear in the agent as `server__tool`. Only tools are served (no resources or prompts), and a tool you turned off in the Library is neither listed nor run.

## Turn it on

1. **Open the page.** Go to Library → MCP.
2. **Switch it on.** Below the server list, turn on MCP router. Each agent that has Library servers ticked and can reach a server over HTTP (Streamable HTTP) gets one `magpie` entry at `/mcp/magpie/hub/<agent>` on magpie’s gateway, and those servers’ own entries are taken out of its config.
3. **Restart your agents.** An agent reads the change when it starts again.

Turning it off writes each server’s own entry back, removes only the `magpie` entry magpie wrote, and stops every server the router started. From the command line:

```
magpie library mcp router on
magpie library mcp router off
```

`magpie library` lists which agents are given the router and which keep their own entries, with why.

## Other apps

With the router on, the Other apps row shows an address ending in `/mcp/magpie/hub`, which serves every server in the Library. Connect… opens a sheet with a ready entry to copy for Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf or any app that takes a JSON MCP config; in the app window, Cursor and VS Code also have Add, which opens the app to confirm. An app on another computer needs a gateway key, as every request from your network does (see [Remote magpie](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/remote)).

> **Command servers run on this computer.** Anyone holding a gateway key on your network can call them through the router, with your rights here. Only share keys with people you trust.

## Agents that keep their own entries

These agents keep each server’s own entry, and the Library page says which and why:

- **No remote servers..** The agent can’t reach an MCP server over HTTP, such as Claude Desktop.
- **A server named magpie..** One of your Library servers is itself called `magpie`, so the names would clash.
- **Its own magpie entry..** The agent already has an entry called `magpie` that magpie didn’t write; it is left as it is.

## When to use it

- **Turn it on.** when you use several agents with the same servers, when command servers start many copies of themselves, or when you want editors and other computers to use your Library.
- **Leave it off.** if you use one agent, if you want each agent to talk to its servers directly, or if you’d rather nothing else on your network can reach your command servers. Every call goes through magpie, so magpie needs to be running.

---

Source: https://usemagpie.ai/docs/remote

# Remote magpie

One magpie can serve several computers. Sign in and set up providers and routing groups once, on the computer that keeps them (your desktop, a server, a [NAS in Docker](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/docker)), and on every other computer add that magpie as a provider of its own: a **Remote magpie**.

|  | The shared magpie | Each other computer’s magpie |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Providers, subscriptions, keys | kept and signed in here | uses them through the Remote magpie |
| Routing groups | made here | picked as `office/group/…` |
| Agents | its own | still wired by this computer’s magpie |
| Usage and quotas | counted and read here | shown here, named with the remote |

The computer you sit at still runs magpie: it wires that computer’s agents, picks their models and keeps their sessions. Only the models come from the other one.

## 1. Share the main magpie

1. **Turn on sharing.** On the computer that keeps your providers: Settings → Network and sharing → Share on local network → On. magpie then listens on the local network and makes a gateway key named Magpie. The Address row below the switch shows where other computers reach it, such as `http://192.168.1.20:3425`.
2. **Make a key for each computer.** Gateway → Gateway keys, or `magpie gateway-key add "Laptop"`, which prints its `sk-magpie-key-…`. Each key can have its own daily, weekly or monthly limit and its own models, and its calls are counted under its name.

While sharing is off, a desktop magpie listens on its own computer only, and other computers can’t reach it. A magpie in Docker is reached through its published port instead, and asks every caller outside its container for a gateway key, shared or not; see [Docker](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/docker#share).

## 2. Add it on the other computer

You need the address and a key from step 1. Any of these does it:

- **The app:.** on the Providers tab press ＋ Add provider, pick Remote magpie under Another computer’s magpie (the last heading), then give its address and the key.
- **The TUI.** (`magpie tui`): on the Providers page press `a`, pick Remote magpie, then type its address and key. On its row, `w` changes the address and `m` fetches its list again.
- **The CLI:.**

```
magpie provider add remote-magpie sk-magpie-key-… url=http://192.168.1.20:3425 id=office
magpie models            # office/… are the shared magpie's
magpie provider refresh office   # fetch its list again
```

`id=` names the provider here, and so begins its models’ ids (`office/…`). The address can be typed as `192.168.1.20:3425` (plain `http://` is assumed), with `/v1` after it, or as the root: magpie puts every API on it either way. Add one Remote magpie for each computer you share from, with a different id.

## What you get

- **Its models.** , as its own agents are shown them: `office/relay-a/claude-sonnet-5`, labelled `Claude Sonnet 5 · Relay A · office`. The ids stay ids; only the labels carry the names. Pick them for an agent here like any other model.
- **Its routing groups.** , as `office/group/…`. The group decides on the shared magpie, with its accounts.
- **Every API..** A request goes on in the API the agent spoke (Anthropic Messages and token counting, Responses, Chat Completions). A model that the shared magpie’s provider serves on another API only is turned into that API once, never on both computers. Responses go over HTTP, SSE included, not WebSocket.
- **Images and video..** Its image and video models are found by themselves and served through its image generation and edit, and video, APIs.
- **System One..** Its decision models (Jev, Clef, and models with names of your own) are set up at its `/v1/systemone` and appear as decision models, not chat models. Refresh the provider’s list to find new ones. A bare `office` asks the first decision model listed.
- **Embeddings, rerank, speech to text and text to speech.** go to its matching APIs. They stay in agents’ lists as they are on the remote; being listed doesn’t make them able to hold a conversation.
- **Prices..** Each model costs here what the shared magpie counts it at (a price set there by hand, else its provider’s list price), so the two computers count the same. A price you set here comes first.

## Quotas and usage

The Usage page, the menu bar and `magpie quota` show the shared magpie’s subscription cards, named with it (`Codex · office`, id `office/codex`), as that magpie last read them: only the computer with the sign-ins asks the vendors. A card’s refresh here has it read that card once more, at most once every 30 seconds. A Codex reset or a WorkBuddy check-in is pressed on that computer, from its own app, TUI or CLI. A key that magpie holds to a budget, some models or some accounts is told none of its cards: only that key’s own card shows here, with its limit.

The shared magpie counts this computer’s requests under the name of the gateway key it sends, with the account that answered.

## Short-lived keys

A program that starts agents in sandboxes can give each one a gateway key of its own that stops working by itself. The key lives 1 minute to 30 days, and may be held to some models, some accounts, a number of tokens or a cost over its whole life, or to read-only use. Its secret is told once, in the answer.

```
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1/magpie/keys \
  -d '{"name":"sandbox-1","ttl":"1h","models":["office/codex/gpt-5"],"tokens":200000}'
# {"id":"k…","name":"sandbox-1","key":"sk-magpie-…","expires":"…","models":[…],"limit":{…}}
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1/magpie/keys              # the keys you issued, masked
curl -s -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1/magpie/keys/k…  # revoke one early
```

A program on this computer may call it with no key; a page in a browser may not. Another computer, a container or CI calls it with a gateway key you let issue keys, and every key it issues is held to that key: never a model or account it may not use, never past its own expiry, and what they spend counts against its limit. Turning it off or removing it stops its keys at once. The same from the command line, which prints the key alone:

```
magpie gateway-key issue --ttl 1h --name sandbox-1 --models office/codex/gpt-5 --tokens 200000
magpie gateway-key issuer <id> on    # let a key issue keys
magpie gateway-key issue --ttl 30m --from <id> --read-only --json
magpie gateway-key list               # until 10-31 14:00, expired, issued by …
```

An expired key is refused with `401` and why (“the gateway key "sandbox-1" expired at …: ask for a new one”) on every API, from this computer too. It is removed an hour later.

## Keys for GitHub Actions

A GitHub Actions job can get a short-lived key without a gateway key in the repository’s secrets: it trades the OIDC token GitHub gives it. Write a rule naming the repository (and, if you like, the branch, environment or any other claim, exact or with `*`), the gateway key its keys are issued under, and how long they live:

```
magpie gateway-key issuer <id> on
magpie gateway-key oidc add --key <id> --repo owner/app --ref refs/heads/main --ttl 1h
# prints the rule id and its audience, magpie-<rule id>
magpie gateway-key oidc list
magpie gateway-key oidc remove <rule id>
```

In the workflow, ask GitHub for a token with the rule’s audience and POST it to `/v1/magpie/keys/oidc`:

```
permissions:
  id-token: write
steps:
  - name: Get a magpie key
    run: |
      TOKEN=$(curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN" \
        "$ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL&audience=magpie-<rule id>" | jq -r .value)
      KEY=$(curl -s -X POST https://<your magpie>/v1/magpie/keys/oidc \
        -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"ttl":"30m"}' | jq -r .key)
      echo "::add-mask::$KEY"
      echo "MAGPIE_KEY=$KEY" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
```

The key is issued under the rule’s gateway key and held to it like any other issued key, lives no longer than the rule says, and is named after the repository, branch and run. A token from another repository or branch, an expired one, or one already traded gets `401` and why. The route answers another computer only while magpie is shared, and refused tokens count against the failed sign-ins it allows. Without a rule nothing is traded.

## Stats API

What the Usage page shows is also served as JSON, to this computer and, while magpie is shared, to a request with a gateway key. A key held to a budget, models or accounts is told only its own calls and limit, and the quotas of what it may use once its owner turns on Quotas for it (`magpie gateway-key quotas <id> on`).

- `/v1/magpie/usage?period=today|7d|30d|all`: totals, by model, agent, provider, account and gateway key.
- `/v1/magpie/usage/requests`: the request log, with `period`, `day`, `offset`, `limit`, and filters `model`, `agent`, `provider`, `account`, `callerKey`, `failed=1`, `retried=1` and `q`.
- `/v1/magpie/quotas`: each subscription’s windows (`?kept=1` without asking the vendors); `/v1/magpie/quotas/history?days=`: what was left over time, 45 days at most.
- `/v1/magpie/limit`: the key’s own limits, its expiry, and its issuer’s limits; for a held key, what holds it (`heldTo`), its `models`, and whether it is told quotas (`quotas`, `quotaProviders`).
- `/v1/magpie/concurrency`: requests in flight, per account.

```
curl -s 'http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1/magpie/usage?period=7d'
curl -s 'http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1/magpie/usage/requests?period=today&callerKey=k…&failed=1&limit=50'
curl -s 'http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1/magpie/quotas?kept=1'
curl -s 'http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1/magpie/quotas/history?days=14'
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1/magpie/limit -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-magpie-…'
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1/magpie/concurrency
```

## When it doesn’t work

| You see | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| “magpie isn’t shared on the local network”, or “remote magpie isn’t shared” | turn on Share on local network on that computer |
| “remote magpie didn’t take this key” (401) | use one of its enabled gateway keys: Gateway → Gateway keys there |
| 403 for a model | that key may use only some models: `magpie gateway-key models <id>` on that computer shows or changes them. A bare `office` asks System One’s first decision model, whatever the key allows; use the full `office/provider/model` id |
| “couldn’t reach the remote magpie” | check the address, that magpie is running there with sharing on, and that its firewall lets the port in |
| no System One models, or “doesn’t share its quotas” | update magpie on that computer, then refresh the list here |

> **Away from home**, reach the shared magpie over a VPN such as Tailscale or WireGuard, with its address there. Don’t open its port to the internet.

Questions or a setup worth sharing? Ask on [Discord](https://discord.gg/vGSnD3ZKQF). The [reference](https://github.com/yetone/magpie/blob/main/docs/reference.md) has the details.

---

Source: https://usemagpie.ai/docs/docker

# magpie in Docker

Run magpie on a server or a NAS that has no desktop: its gateway serves your models to agents on other computers, and you add providers and sign in to subscriptions from a page in your browser.

| **Image** | `ghcr.io/yetone/magpie`, for `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64` |
| --- | --- |
| **Tags** | `latest` (the newest release), `daily` (the newest release as of 20:00 UTC, moved once a day), `stable` (the desktop app's Stable channel: a release a week, out three days first, or an urgent one at once), `0.1.1150` (one release), `0.1`, `edge` (every change on `main`) |
| **Ports** | `3425` the gateway agents call; `3430` the browser UI, when the container runs `magpie web`; it answers the gateway’s `/v1` routes too, so a reverse proxy needs only this port |
| **Volume** | `/config`: providers, keys, sign-ins, plugins and usage |
| **User** | nonroot (uid 65532) |

The image holds magpie’s terminal-only build on Debian 12 slim, with bash for a terminal in the container and curl for the installers of the CLIs some subscriptions sign in with (Cursor, Devin, Grok Build). It runs `magpie serve` (the gateway alone) unless given another command. The container finds no agents to wire, so magpie in it is a gateway: the agents that use it run elsewhere.

## Run it

Run it with the browser UI, a key for that page you keep across restarts, and both ports on the host’s loopback only:

```
docker run -d --name magpie --restart unless-stopped \
  -p 127.0.0.1:3425:3425 -p 127.0.0.1:3430:3430 \
  -e MAGPIE_WEB_KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 16) \
  -v magpie-config:/config \
  ghcr.io/yetone/magpie:latest web --addr 0.0.0.0:3430 --no-open

docker logs magpie
```

The log names the page with its key:

```
● magpie web on http://127.0.0.1:3430/?k=0f3c9a1e…
  on the network http://172.17.0.2:3430/?k=0f3c9a1e…
  these are the container's own addresses: other machines use the host's, and MAGPIE_PUBLIC_URL=http://<host>:<port> puts it here
  other containers on this host http://172.17.0.1:3425
! anyone with the link can change magpie and see its keys, and the network carries it unencrypted
  the link carries MAGPIE_WEB_KEY · gateway http://127.0.0.1:3425 · Ctrl-C to stop
```

> **Agents outside the container need a gateway key.** In the container any key works. A request from the host or another machine is answered only with an enabled gateway key, and gets 401 without one: make one as in Gateway keys. `127.0.0.1:` in `-p` keeps a port on the host; leave it out, or name the host’s LAN or VPN address, for other machines to reach it.

Without `web --addr 0.0.0.0:3430 --no-open` the container runs the gateway alone, which you then set up from a terminal in it (`docker exec -it magpie magpie provider add …`). A folder bind-mounted at `/config` works in place of the named volume, if uid 65532 can write it: `sudo chown -R 65532:65532 /volume1/docker/magpie/config`.

## The browser UI

Open the link from the log. The key in it is traded for a cookie and taken out of the address; a page opened without it is turned away (401). With `MAGPIE_WEB_KEY` set (16 or more letters, digits or `- . _ ~`; `openssl rand -hex 16` makes one) the key stays the same across restarts and the browser stays signed in for 400 days. Without it, every start makes a new key and the cookie lasts the browser session.

The page is in **gateway mode**: Providers, Gateway, Routing, Usage, Sessions, Plugins and Settings, with no Agents, since there are no agents in the container. Library has its MCP servers alone, with the MCP router: other computers’ apps connect at the router’s address with a gateway key. Sessions lists only the sessions of agents on other computers that came through this gateway, never this machine’s agents’ files. Settings → General → Gateway mode turns it off.

On a NAS or a server you reach over SSH, open the page through a tunnel rather than publishing 3430: `ssh -L 3430:127.0.0.1:3430 you@nas`, then the log’s link on your own computer.

> **Anyone with the link can change magpie and see its keys.** Keep 3430 on loopback or a VPN. Across the network, serve it over HTTPS: give magpie a certificate with `MAGPIE_TLS_CERT` and `MAGPIE_TLS_KEY`, or put it behind a reverse proxy with TLS, such as Caddy.

## Sign in to subscriptions

Add API keys on Providers as on the desktop. A subscription’s sign-in (ChatGPT, Claude…) opens the vendor’s page in your browser, and when you are done the vendor sends that browser back to `localhost`, for ChatGPT `http://localhost:1455/auth/callback?code=…`. That is your own computer, not the container, so the page doesn’t load. Copy its whole address from the address bar and paste it into the sign-in’s Callback URL field.

The same from a terminal:

```
docker exec -it magpie magpie accounts add codex
```

Open the link it prints, sign in, then paste the address the browser ended on. The browser UI can also import sign-ins from a file.

A Claude subscription is signed in to and answered through Claude Code, which the image doesn’t have. Have magpie download Anthropic’s own build first: it says the version, where it comes from and where it goes, asks, and checks the download’s SHA-256 against Anthropic’s manifest. It is kept in `/config/cache`, on the volume, so a new image keeps it, and magpie keeps it at Claude Code’s newest release by itself: it looks a minute after it starts and every six hours, and downloads a newer one the same way. Nothing needs installing again after an update. To hold a version, set `-e DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER=1`. `magpie accounts add claude` offers it too when Claude Code is missing.

```
docker exec -it magpie magpie claude-code install
```

A Grok (SuperGrok) subscription signs in through xAI’s Grok Build CLI, which the image doesn’t have either. Its sign-in, in the browser UI or with `magpie plugin login grok`, installs it first, as xAI’s installer does: the stable version from `x.ai/cli`, kept in `/config/home/.grok`. To use a Grok Build binary you put on the volume yourself, set `GROK_BIN_DIR` to the folder holding it.

## Your own browser

Magpie Browser lets agents act in your own browser, through its extension. The extension can’t be loaded from the container’s folders, so in the browser UI open Library → Magpie Browser and click Download the extension. The zip is pointed at the page’s own address, with a gateway key named **Magpie Browser** of its own. Unzip it, open `chrome://extensions`, turn on Developer mode and click Load unpacked on the unzipped folder. An extension already loaded takes the address (`http://localhost:3430`, or the gateway’s published port) and a gateway key in its popup.

The Magpie Browser key connects the extension and nothing else: it can’t use models, MCP servers or stats, so a copy of the zip left in Downloads spends nothing. The host’s browser reaches the container from Docker’s bridge, not from the container’s own computer, so it is that key’s alone and the container’s agents don’t use it yet ([#5529](https://github.com/yetone/magpie/issues/5529)). To use it from an agent on the host, give that agent a gateway key of its own with full access, connect the extension with the same key in its popup, and call `/mcp/magpie/browser` with it. A browser given another key is that key’s alone, and it is let go once its key is turned off, removed or rotated.

## What is kept

Everything magpie writes is under `/config`, so a restart, or a new container on the same volume, keeps your providers, keys, sign-ins and plugins.

| Path | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `/config/magpie` | magpie’s own files: `settings.json`, providers, gateway keys, routing groups |
| `/config/home` | the container’s `HOME`: sign-ins kept where their agent keeps them (`~/.codex`, `~/.claude`…) |
| `/config/cache` | the model catalog, Bun, which plugins run on (downloaded the first time one is used), and the Claude Code `magpie claude-code install` downloaded |
| `/config/data`, `/config/state` | the rest of what magpie keeps |

A volume made by an older image keeps working: magpie adds the folders it lacks when it starts. Only sign-ins made with that older image, which lived outside the volume, have to be made again.

## Environment

| Variable | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `MAGPIE_ADDR` | where the gateway listens. The image sets `0.0.0.0:3425`, so the published port reaches it. |
| `MAGPIE_PUBLIC_URL` | the address other machines reach the gateway at, such as `http://192.168.1.20:3425` (the host’s or the NAS’s, on the published port), or a reverse proxy’s base URL. In the container magpie sees only Docker’s own `172.17.x` address; with this set, the address it shows and prints is the one to use. |
| `MAGPIE_WEB_KEY` | the browser UI’s key, kept across restarts (16+ characters) |
| `MAGPIE_TLS_CERT`, `MAGPIE_TLS_KEY` | a PEM certificate (its chain after it) and its key, mounted into the container: other machines then reach the gateway and the browser UI over `https://` only, and plain HTTP from them gets 400. The files are read again when they change, so a renewal needs no restart. One without the other, or files that don’t load, stop magpie from starting. Use `https://` in `MAGPIE_PUBLIC_URL` too. |
| `MAGPIE_ALLOW_IPS` | the only addresses other machines may reach the gateway and the browser UI from, as IPs and CIDR ranges: `203.0.113.7,10.0.0.0/8,2001:db8::/32`. Any other address gets 403, even with a gateway key. Unset lets every address in, each with a key. See Allowed addresses. |
| `HOME`, `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, `XDG_CACHE_HOME`, `XDG_DATA_HOME`, `XDG_STATE_HOME` | set by the image to the folders under `/config` above; leave them |

## Gateway keys and other machines

1. **Make a key for each client.** Gateway → Gateway keys, or in a terminal `docker exec magpie magpie gateway-key add "Laptop"`, which prints the new `sk-magpie-key-…`. Every request from outside the container, the host’s own included, must carry an enabled gateway key, and one without gets 401. A key can have its own daily, weekly, monthly, every-N-days or every-N-hours limit and its own list of models (`magpie gateway-key limit`, `magpie gateway-key models`).
2. **Publish the port.** Recreate the container with `-p 3425:3425`, or bound to the NAS’s LAN or VPN address (`-p 192.168.1.20:3425:3425`), and with `-e MAGPIE_PUBLIC_URL=http://192.168.1.20:3425`.

On each other computer, point the agent at the gateway with one of those keys as its API key: `http://192.168.1.20:3425/v1` for an OpenAI client, `http://192.168.1.20:3425` for an Anthropic or Gemini one. Model ids are `provider/model`, or a routing group’s; `GET /v1/models` lists them. If that computer runs magpie itself, add the container as a [Remote magpie](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/remote) instead, and magpie wires its agents for you.

**Other containers on the same host.** Another container on the NAS reaches magpie at the host, through the Docker bridge’s gateway and the published port: `http://172.17.0.1:3425` on Docker’s default bridge. The container’s own `172.17.x` address is no use to it, and the host’s LAN address may not be either, as a NAS’s firewall can keep containers from it. `host.docker.internal` is the same address on Docker Desktop, and on Linux only in a container given `extra_hosts: ["host.docker.internal:host-gateway"]`. A container on magpie’s own compose network, or one you made, can use its name, `http://magpie:3425`. Either way it sends a gateway key. The log and the browser UI list this address as Other containers on this host, after the host’s address the page was opened at.

Settings → Network and sharing → Share on local network isn’t needed in the container: turning it on also makes a gateway key named Magpie, and the gateway asks for a key from outside the container either way.

**Upgrading from an earlier image.** An agent outside the container that sends `magpie`, or any other key that isn’t an enabled gateway key, now gets 401 (“the API key sent is not an enabled magpie gateway key”). Make it a key as above and put that in the agent’s settings. Agents that already send a gateway key, and a Remote magpie set up with one, keep working.

**Allowed addresses.** On a public host, set `-e MAGPIE_ALLOW_IPS=203.0.113.7,10.0.0.0/8` to the addresses your clients come from. A request from any other address is refused 403 before its key is looked at, so a key that leaks is no use from elsewhere; the refusal names the address it came from, as does the container’s log. magpie judges the address of the connection itself, never an `X-Forwarded-For` header, and a mistyped entry lets nothing in rather than everything. Docker’s default bridge network passes a client’s own address into the container, but a request from the host itself arrives from the bridge’s gateway (`172.17.0.1`), and Docker Desktop and rootless Docker show every client as one address of their own: add that, or check what the 403 says. Behind a reverse proxy or tunnel, every request comes from the proxy’s address, so limit who reaches magpie at the proxy. On the desktop app the same list is Settings → Network and sharing → Allowed addresses.

> **Over the internet, prefer a VPN** such as Tailscale or WireGuard to opening 3425. A reverse proxy or tunnel in front of the container is the network too: its clients need a gateway key like any other machine’s.

**Claude Code’s status line, with Claude Code outside the container.** The status line square can’t reach another machine’s `~/.claude/settings.json`, and the command it writes names a binary in the container. The gateway answers the same line itself: on the machine Claude Code runs on, set `statusLine` in `~/.claude/settings.json` to `{"type": "command", "command": "curl -fsS -m 1 -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-magpie-key-…' --data-binary @- http://<host>:3425/v1/magpie/statusline || true"}`, with the host or address that reaches the container and a gateway key (a read-only key is enough). A key held to a budget, models or accounts gets the line once its owner turns on Quotas for it, with only the accounts it may use. Add `?format=json` for the same as JSON (the line, the model, and each account’s windows with `used` and `resetsAt`), for a status line that draws its own. Claude Code runs it on every message and passes its session on stdin, which adds the model the session went to. The same command is shown in the browser UI under Settings → About.

## Docker Compose on a NAS

```
services:
  magpie:
    image: ghcr.io/yetone/magpie:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      # 127.0.0.1: the host alone; every caller outside the container needs a gateway key
      - "127.0.0.1:3425:3425"
      - "127.0.0.1:3430:3430"
    environment:
      MAGPIE_PUBLIC_URL: http://<nas-address>:3425
      MAGPIE_WEB_KEY: <random-key>
    volumes:
      - ./config:/config
    command: [web, --addr, 0.0.0.0:3430, --no-open]
```

Then: `sudo chown -R 65532:65532 ./config`, `docker compose up -d`, open `http://127.0.0.1:3430/?k=<random-key>` through an SSH tunnel, add your providers and make a gateway key for each machine. For other machines to reach the gateway, change its line to `"3425:3425"` (or the NAS’s LAN or VPN address) and run `docker compose up -d` again.

## Health, terminal, updates

- **Health..** The image has a `HEALTHCHECK`: `magpie healthcheck` exits 0 while the gateway answers, under `serve` and `web` alike, so `docker ps` shows the container as healthy and Compose can wait for it with `depends_on: condition: service_healthy`.
- **Terminal..** `docker exec -it magpie bash`, or a NAS panel’s terminal, opens a shell with `magpie` on its PATH: `magpie providers`, `magpie models`, `magpie usage`, `magpie quota` and the rest of the [CLI](https://github.com/yetone/magpie/blob/main/docs/reference.md).
- **Updates..** Pull the new image and recreate the container on the same volume: `docker pull ghcr.io/yetone/magpie:latest`, then `docker rm -f magpie` and the same `docker run`, or `docker compose pull && docker compose up -d`. magpie releases several times a day; for one update a day with Renovate or Watchtower, follow `daily` (with Renovate, pin its digest), or `stable` for one a week.
- **Build it yourself..** `docker build -t magpie .` in a checkout of [the repository](https://github.com/yetone/magpie) makes the same image.

Questions or a setup worth sharing? Ask on [Discord](https://discord.gg/vGSnD3ZKQF). The [reference](https://github.com/yetone/magpie/blob/main/docs/reference.md#docker) has the details.

---

Source: https://usemagpie.ai/docs/import

# Add to magpie

Hand your users one link, and your models show up in every agent they run: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Pi, Crush. No config files, no environment variables, no copy-pasting base URLs.

## Quick start

1. **Build a link.** Describe your endpoint as URL parameters: a name, a base URL per API you speak, and optionally the user’s key and the models to offer.
2. **Put it behind a button.** On your dashboard, next to the key you just minted: *Add to magpie*.
3. **The user confirms.** magpie opens, shows exactly where prompts and the key will go, and adds the provider when the user says yes. Every agent can use it right away.

```
https://usemagpie.ai/import#name=Acme%20Relay&chat=https://api.acme.example/v1&anthropic=https://api.acme.example&key=sk-…&models=gpt-5.5,claude-sonnet-5
```

## The link

magpie registers the `magpie://` scheme with the system. An import link is that scheme, the word `import`, and a query string:

On the web, link to the same parameters on `usemagpie.ai/import` instead, after a `#`:

### Why the https link

It works everywhere a link does: GitHub READMEs, chat apps and email clients drop or block custom schemes. It opens magpie, and offers the download when magpie isn’t installed yet.

### Why after the `#`

Browsers never send the fragment to a server. The key goes from your page to the user’s machine without passing through usemagpie.ai, not even its logs.

Every value is URL-encoded, as `URLSearchParams` or `urlencode` produce. Both `%20` and `+` work for spaces.

## Parameters

A link either names one of magpie’s presets, which already knows the vendor’s endpoints, or describes a provider from scratch with a name and at least one base URL.

| Parameter | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `name`or preset | What the provider is called in magpie, at most 80 characters. |
| `chat` | OpenAI Chat Completions base URL, ending in `/v1` (magpie appends `/chat/completions`). |
| `responses` | OpenAI Responses base URL, ending in `/v1`. Codex speaks only this API; magpie translates for it when you don’t. |
| `anthropic` | Anthropic Messages base URL: the root, without `/v1`. |
| `gemini` | Google Gemini API base URL, ending in `/v1beta`, as the app’s editor and the TUI take one. |
| `key` | The user’s API key. Leave it out and the user pastes one in the dialog. |
| `models` | Model ids to offer the agents, comma separated. Without it, magpie lists the models your `/v1/models` returns. |
| `id` | The id agents use in `id/model`. Defaults to the name, lowercased with dashes (`Acme Relay` → `acme-relay`). |
| `catalog` | A [models.dev](https://models.dev) provider id whose metadata applies, e.g. `openai` for a relay of OpenAI models: display names, context sizes (written into the agents that take them), reasoning levels and image input; the model list when the provider’s own `/models` can’t be read; and per-token prices, which the Usage page turns into a cost estimate in USD. Several ids may be given, comma-separated: their models are combined, and where two know the same model the first one’s entry is used. |
| `website` | Your site (https). Shown on the provider’s page. |
| `keys` | The page where users make keys (https). The dialog links to it when the link has no key. |
| `icon` | A picture of your own (https): PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, ICO or SVG, at most 1 MB. magpie downloads it once, after the user confirms the import, and keeps it beside the provider. Without one, magpie shows the `catalog` vendor’s logo or a plain mark. |
| `balance` | Where the key’s balance is read (https), on the host of one of your base URLs: magpie asks it with the key, as a chat request sends it. `{key}` in it stands for the key. Without it, magpie reads the vendors it knows, and asks a relay where new-api and sub2api tell a key its balance (`/api/usage/token`, `/v1/usage`); give one when yours answers elsewhere. |
| `balance_path` | Where the amount is in the JSON reply: a dotted path, list items by index (`data.balance`, `balance_infos.0.total_balance`), or a sum of them in your own units (`$ data.quota / 500000`). `$` or `¥` before it is the currency, `%` after it a percent of 1; several amounts go apart by `;`, each with a `label:` if wanted. Needs `balance`. |
| `balance_method` | `GET`, the default, or `POST` with no body. Needs `balance`. |
| `preset`or name | A preset id; its endpoints, catalog and pages are used, and `name` may rename it. |
| `region` | With a preset that has regions, which one. |

At least one of `chat`, `responses`, `anthropic` and `gemini` is required without a preset; give every API you speak, and each agent uses the one it speaks natively. Base URLs must be **https**, except plain http to `localhost`, loopback, private addresses and `*.local`, where model servers usually run without TLS. They can’t carry a query, a fragment or credentials.

A link sets no other header or token for the balance: an account-wide access token is worth more than one key, and a URL stays in browser history. A balance that needs one is set up in the provider’s editor.

### Presets

Vendors magpie already knows. `magpie presets` prints the current list.

A vendor with a preset only needs to add the key: `magpie://import?preset=deepseek&key=sk-…`. Want yours on the list? [Open an issue](https://github.com/yetone/magpie/issues).

## Link builder

Fill in your endpoint; the link, the button and the Markdown follow as you type. Everything stays in this page.

## The button

Two ready-made badges, one for light pages and one for dark. Link them to your import link, or draw your own button: the words *Add to magpie* and the bird are yours to use.

```
<a href="https://usemagpie.ai/import#preset=deepseek&key=sk-…">
  <img src="https://usemagpie.ai/img/add-to-magpie.svg" alt="Add to magpie" width="176" height="40">
</a>
```

```
[![Add to magpie](https://usemagpie.ai/img/add-to-magpie.svg)](https://usemagpie.ai/import#preset=deepseek)
```

For dark pages, use `add-to-magpie-light.svg`. A public page like a README should never carry a key; leave `key` out and the user pastes their own.

## From your backend

The natural place for the button is the page that shows a freshly minted key. Build the link where you have it:

```
const params = new URLSearchParams({
  name: "Acme Relay",
  chat: "https://api.acme.example/v1",
  anthropic: "https://api.acme.example",
  key: apiKey,
  models: ["gpt-5.5", "claude-sonnet-5"].join(","),
  icon: "https://acme.example/logo.svg",
});
const href = "https://usemagpie.ai/import#" + params;
```

```
from urllib.parse import urlencode

href = "https://usemagpie.ai/import#" + urlencode({
    "name": "Acme Relay",
    "chat": "https://api.acme.example/v1",
    "anthropic": "https://api.acme.example",
    "key": api_key,
    "models": "gpt-5.5,claude-sonnet-5",
    "icon": "https://acme.example/logo.svg",
})
```

```
magpie import 'magpie://import?preset=deepseek&key=sk-…'   # asks first; -y to skip
```

## Security

An import link is a suggestion. The user decides.

- **Always confirmed..** magpie shows the name, every host that prompts and the key will go to, and the models, and saves nothing until the user presses Add. The user can rename it, or replace the key, first.
- **No silent overwrites..** When the id is already taken, the dialog says so and the button reads *Replace*.
